courses.name: How computers work
courses.blurb: Number systems, hardware, what an OS does, and just enough basic electronics to read a circuit.

modules.note: Voltage is push, current is flow, resistance is opposition. Ohm's law: V = I x R. Power: P = V x I. Series resistors add; parallel resistors share current. A resistor in series with an LED sets its current. Practice on a breadboard or a free simulator.

courses.name: Hardware and basic EE
courses.blurb: Ohm's law, basic circuits, how the CPU, RAM and storage connect, and the boot chain. Basic electronics only, no gate-level logic.

modules.note:
Voltage (volts, V) is the push between two points. Current (amps, A) is the flow of charge. Resistance (ohms) is how much a part opposes the flow. Ohm's law ties them together: V = I x R, so I = V / R and R = V / I. Example: 12 V across 4 kilohms gives 3 mA.

Power (watts) is P = V x I. Combined with Ohm's law, P = I^2 x R = V^2 / R. A resistor must be rated for the power it burns: 5 V across 1 kilohm is 5 mA and 25 mW, fine for a 1/4 W part. Heat is where wasted power goes.

DC has a fixed polarity (batteries, USB, every chip's supply). AC reverses direction (wall power). Chips run on low-voltage DC; the power supply in a PC converts AC to DC. Read the units carefully: milli = 1/1000, kilo = 1000, micro = 1/1,000,000.

links.t: Falstad circuit simulator (free, in the browser)

modules.note:
Series: parts in a chain. The same current flows through all of them and resistances add (R = R1 + R2 + ...). Voltage splits in proportion to resistance. Parallel: parts across the same two points. Each branch sees the same voltage, currents add, and the combined resistance is lower than the smallest branch (1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2; for two parts, R = R1 x R2 / (R1 + R2)).

Voltage divider: two resistors in series split the input, Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2). It is how sensors and reference levels are made. LEDs: past their forward voltage (about 2 V red, 3 V blue) they conduct freely, so always add a series resistor, R = (Vsupply - Vf) / I. A 5 V supply, a 2 V LED and 10 mA needs 300 ohms.

Meter use: measure voltage in parallel, current in series (break the circuit), resistance with the part unpowered. Never put an ammeter across a supply. A solderless breadboard connects the five holes in each short row; power rails run the length of the board. Build the LED circuit in a simulator first, then on a real breadboard if you have one.

modules.t: How the CPU, RAM and storage connect
modules.note:
The CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute forever. The program counter holds the next instruction's address; registers hold the working values; the ALU does the math. Everything outside the CPU is slower, so there is a hierarchy: registers (under 1 ns), L1/L2/L3 cache (SRAM, a few ns), RAM (DRAM, about 100 ns), SSD (about 100 microseconds), hard disk (milliseconds). Caches work because programs reuse nearby data and recent data (locality).

The CPU talks to RAM over memory channels and to everything else over PCIe lanes, either directly or through the chipset. NVMe SSDs sit on PCIe; SATA drives use an older interface designed for spinning disks; USB and Ethernet reach the CPU through controllers. Devices can use DMA to move data into RAM without the CPU copying each byte, then raise an interrupt when done. Address width sets the ceiling: 32 bits reach 4 GiB, 64 bits far more.

Security link: the same view explains why a malicious PCIe or Thunderbolt device can read memory unless an IOMMU limits DMA, and why exploits aim at the program counter. No gate-level logic is needed here; the goal is a mental map of the box.

Power on: the firmware (UEFI on modern machines, legacy BIOS on old ones) runs POST, initializes hardware, then loads a bootloader from the EFI system partition or the disk's first sector. The bootloader loads the kernel, and the kernel starts the init system and your login screen. Disks use MBR (2 TiB limit with 512-byte sectors, 4 primary partitions) or GPT (64-bit addressing, backup header, required by UEFI boot).

Secure Boot makes the firmware check a signature on each stage before running it. A TPM is a small tamper-resistant chip that holds keys and records measurements of the boot chain, so BitLocker can refuse to release the disk key if the chain changed. Bootkits and firmware implants load before the OS and hide from it, which is why defenders watch the chain itself.

Practical hardening for a laptop: set a firmware password, lock the boot order to the internal disk, turn on Secure Boot, and use full-disk encryption. Anyone with ten minutes and a USB stick can otherwise read an unencrypted disk.

courses.name: Operating systems
courses.blurb: Processes, scheduling, virtual memory, file systems, concurrency and deadlock, with scheduler, paging and Banker's simulators.

modules.note:
A program is a file; a process is a running instance with its own address space (code, globals, heap, stack), open files and a process ID. The kernel tracks each in a process control block (PCB). States: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked on I/O), terminated. A context switch saves one process's registers and program counter into its PCB and loads another's.

On Unix a new process starts with fork(), which copies the caller and returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. exec() replaces the current program image with a new one; wait() collects the exit status. That is how a shell runs a command: fork, exec in the child, wait in the parent. A child that exited but was not waited for is a zombie; a child whose parent died is an orphan, adopted by init.

Threads live inside a process and share the heap, globals and open files, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter. That makes them cheap and also dangerous: shared memory needs locks. Processes talk through IPC: pipes, sockets, signals, shared memory. User code asks the kernel for services through system calls, a controlled trap into kernel mode. On Linux, try `strace ls` to watch them.

The scheduler picks which ready process gets the CPU. Metrics: turnaround = completion - arrival; waiting = turnaround - burst; response = first run - arrival. Policies: FCFS (simple, suffers the convoy effect, where short jobs wait behind a long one); SJF (shortest next burst first, minimizes average waiting time but needs burst lengths and can starve long jobs); SRTF (the preemptive version); priority (aging prevents starvation); round robin (each job gets a fixed quantum, good response time, quantum too big becomes FCFS and too small drowns in switching); multilevel feedback queue (start high, demote CPU hogs, keeps interactive jobs snappy without knowing lengths).

Worked example: bursts 24, 3, 3, all arriving at time 0. FCFS waits are 0, 24, 27, average 17. SJF runs 3, 3, 24 for waits 0, 3, 6, average 3. Do it by hand first, then check it in the simulator; change the quantum and watch round robin move between the two.

Each process sees its own virtual address space. The hardware MMU translates virtual to physical addresses using page tables: memory is cut into pages (usually 4 KiB), and a virtual address splits into a virtual page number and an offset. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KiB pages the offset is 12 bits and there are 2^20 page numbers, so real systems use multi-level tables. The TLB caches recent translations.

Pages need not all be in RAM. Touching a valid page that is on disk causes a page fault, and the OS loads it (demand paging). When RAM is full something must be evicted: FIFO, LRU, clock, and the unbuildable optimal (OPT) used as a yardstick. FIFO can get worse with more frames (Belady's anomaly): the string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. If working sets exceed RAM the machine thrashes. Copy-on-write lets fork() share pages until one side writes.

Security link: page permissions give the NX bit (data is not executable) and let the OS keep user code out of kernel memory. ASLR randomizes the layout so exploits can't hard-code addresses. Segmentation faults are the OS stopping a bad access.

A Unix file is an inode: owner, permissions, size, timestamps and pointers to data blocks. The name is not in the inode; a directory is a table of name-to-inode entries. So one inode can have several names (hard links, tracked by a link count), and a symbolic link is a tiny file holding a path. Deleting a file removes a name; when the link count reaches zero the blocks are marked free, but the data usually stays on disk until reused, which is what forensic recovery relies on. Space after a file's last byte in its final block is slack space.

An inode typically holds 12 direct pointers and then single, double and triple indirect blocks. With 4 KiB blocks and 4-byte pointers: direct covers 48 KiB, single indirect 1024 x 4 KiB = 4 MiB, double indirect 4 GiB. Alternatives are contiguous allocation (fast, fragments) and linked allocation (FAT).

A crash halfway through an update can leave the filesystem inconsistent. Journaling filesystems (ext4, NTFS) log the change first and replay it after a crash. Permissions: rwx for owner, group and others, e.g. 640 is rw-r-----. Mount points and the VFS layer let many filesystems appear in one tree.

A race condition is when the result depends on how threads interleave. counter++ compiles to load, add, store, so two threads can both load 5 and both store 6. The region that touches shared state is the critical section, and it needs mutual exclusion.

Tools: a mutex (lock/unlock); a semaphore, a counter with atomic wait (decrement, block at 0) and signal (increment); condition variables to sleep until something changes; monitors that bundle a lock with its conditions. Hardware supplies atomic instructions: test-and-set and compare-and-swap (CAS). A spinlock busy-waits and is right only for very short holds; a mutex puts the thread to sleep.

Classic problems: producer/consumer (semaphores empty = N, full = 0, plus a mutex), readers/writers, dining philosophers. Each exists to practice reasoning about ordering. Security link: TOCTOU. A program that checks a file with access() and then opens it can be raced by an attacker who swaps in a symlink. Operate on one file descriptor instead of re-resolving a name.

Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one and it cannot happen. Prevention in practice: lock ordering (every thread takes locks in the same global order) kills circular wait; take-all-or-nothing kills hold and wait; try-lock with backoff avoids waiting forever. Detection: build a wait-for graph and look for a cycle, then recover by killing or rolling back a process. Livelock is when threads keep reacting to each other without progress; starvation is when one never gets the resource.

Avoidance with the Banker's algorithm: each process declares its maximum need; need = max - allocation. A state is safe if some order exists where every process can finish. Grant a request only if the resulting state is still safe. Example: available (3,3,2); P1 needs (1,2,2), which fits, so P1 can finish and return its resources, and the sequence continues. The simulator finds a safe sequence for you.

Protection starts in hardware: user mode and kernel mode (rings). User code can't run privileged instructions or touch kernel memory; it asks through system calls. The kernel then checks permissions: DAC (owners set access, normal Unix and Windows ACLs) and MAC (a central policy such as SELinux or AppArmor that owners can't override). Least privilege means each process and account gets only what it needs.

Privilege escalation targets the gaps: setuid-root programs (`find / -perm -4000`), sudo misconfigurations, writable service files, vulnerable drivers. Exploit mitigations make memory bugs harder: NX/DEP, ASLR, stack canaries, RELRO, control-flow integrity. Isolation: containers use namespaces (what a process sees) and cgroups (what it can use) but share the host kernel, so a kernel bug breaks them; VMs add a hypervisor boundary.

A kernel-level rootkit can lie to user-mode tools about files and processes, which is why defenders use memory forensics and offline scans. Pair this module with the hardening guide and run the checklist on your own machine.

courses.name: Databases
courses.blurb: Relational model, normalization, indexes, query plans, transactions and database security, with a dependency tool, an index demo and a serializability checker.

modules.note:
Data lives in relations (tables) of tuples (rows) over attributes (columns). A superkey identifies a row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey; the primary key is the candidate you choose; a foreign key must match a row in another table or be NULL (referential integrity). Relational algebra is the theory under SQL: selection picks rows (WHERE), projection picks columns (SELECT list), join combines tables.

Refresh the core: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregates. INNER JOIN keeps matches only; LEFT JOIN keeps every left row, filling NULLs, and `WHERE right.id IS NULL` finds rows with no match. NULL is unknown, so `= NULL` never matches; use IS NULL. Know the logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Practice in the SQL guide's shell before continuing.

Bad design causes anomalies: update (the same fact stored in many rows, change one and miss another), insert (cannot record a fact without an unrelated one), delete (removing a row loses an unrelated fact). Normalization removes them using functional dependencies: A -> B means rows that agree on A agree on B.

1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependency (a non-key column depending on only part of a composite key). 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency (a non-key column determined by another non-key column). BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key. A handy rule: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

Example: Orders(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name, customer_id, customer_email) with key (order_id, product_id). product_name depends on product_id alone (partial). customer_email depends on customer_id (transitive). Split into orders, order_lines, products, customers. Model many-to-many with a junction table. Denormalize only on purpose, for measured read speed. Use the dependency tool to find keys and the highest normal form.

An index is a separate sorted structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table. Most are B-trees: shallow and wide, so one lookup in millions of rows is a handful of page reads (O(log n)) and range scans and ORDER BY come free. Hash indexes are O(1) for equality but have no ordering. A clustered index defines the physical row order (one per table); non-clustered indexes point back to rows. A covering index holds every column the query needs, so the table isn't touched.

Rules of thumb: a composite index (a, b) helps filters on a or on a and b, not b alone (leftmost prefix). A function on the column (UPPER(name), DATE(ts)) or a leading wildcard (LIKE '%son') usually defeats the index. Index the columns you filter, join and sort on. Low selectivity (a boolean) rarely pays. Every index slows writes and costs space, so do not index everything. Primary keys and unique constraints get one automatically; foreign keys often don't.

The optimizer turns a query into a plan: access method for each table (sequential scan, index scan, index-only scan), join algorithm, join order. Nested loop join: for each outer row probe the inner, great with an index on the inner side. Hash join: build a hash table of one input, probe with the other, good for big equality joins. Merge join: both inputs sorted, walk them together. The optimizer picks the cheapest from row-count estimates based on statistics (run ANALYZE after big changes).

Read plans with EXPLAIN (add ANALYZE in PostgreSQL for real timings). Red flags: a sequential scan on a large table for a selective filter, estimated rows far from actual rows, a sort that spills to disk, a nested loop over millions of rows. Fix loop: look at the plan, add or change an index, re-run, compare. Write queries so the optimizer can use indexes: compare the bare column to a constant, avoid SELECT * when a narrow covering index would do.

A transaction is a group of statements treated as one unit (BEGIN ... COMMIT or ROLLBACK). ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), Durability (committed data survives a crash).

Durability and atomicity come from write-ahead logging: log the change to disk first, then apply it; after a crash, redo committed work and undo the rest. Isolation levels trade safety for speed: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads; READ COMMITTED stops them; REPEATABLE READ also stops non-repeatable reads; SERIALIZABLE also stops phantoms and behaves as if transactions ran one at a time. Implementations use two-phase locking or MVCC, where readers see a snapshot and don't block writers. Concurrent locks can deadlock; the database aborts one victim, so applications should retry.

A schedule is conflict-serializable if its precedence graph (an edge Ti -> Tj when an operation of Ti conflicts with and precedes one of Tj) has no cycle. Try some in the checker.

SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a query so it's parsed as SQL. The fix is parameterized queries (prepared statements), which keep data separate from code. Escaping by hand is fragile. Add least privilege: the web app's account gets only the statements and tables it needs, never DROP or file-write rights. NoSQL stores have the same problem in a different shape, e.g. operator injection with {"$ne": null} in a login query.

Store passwords as salted hashes from a slow algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2), never reversible encryption. Encrypt data at rest to protect stolen disks and backups, and use TLS in transit; neither stops injection. Turn on auditing, patch the engine, don't expose the port to the internet, remove default accounts. Backups: keep copies offline or immutable so ransomware with database credentials can't destroy them, and test a restore before you need it.

courses.blurb: Why many machines are harder than one: replication, CAP, consensus with Raft, queues and a simulated 3-node cluster you can break.

links.t: ~/dist: queues and streams (lab: the double charge)

modules.note: Run the five experiments on the cluster page: crash the leader, lose the majority, isolate the leader and heal, a stale read in AP mode, and last-write-wins. For each, write down what you expected before you press the button.

courses.blurb: A short linear algebra refresher, regression, classifiers and honest evaluation, with a model you train in the browser. Security examples throughout.

courses.name: Programming languages
courses.blurb: What separates languages: paradigms, static and dynamic types, scope and closures, and functional programming. ~/code and ~/dojo are the reps.

courses.name: Compilers
courses.blurb: How source text becomes a running program: the pipeline, a lexer, a recursive-descent parser and a tree-walking interpreter you finish yourself.

modules.note: Stretch goal after the lab: add an if statement and a function call to the calculator language, then read the first half of Crafting Interpreters.

courses.name: Theory of computation (optional)
courses.blurb: Light and optional: automata and regular expressions, context-free grammars, Turing machines, the halting problem and what NP means. No discrete math prerequisite.

courses.name: Network+
courses.blurb: Network+ N10-009 domains, from concepts to troubleshooting.

courses.name: Network security
courses.blurb: Firewalls, IDS, VPNs and reading traffic.

courses.name: Virtualization and homelab ops
courses.blurb: Proxmox, a segmented lab, hardening and keeping servers alive.

courses.name: Cloud and cloud security
courses.blurb: AWS and Azure side by side: identity, networking, storage and what breaks.

courses.name: Logs and SIEM
courses.blurb: Reading logs, shaping them with pipes and regex, and working a SIEM.

courses.name: Incident response and forensics
courses.blurb: The IR lifecycle, disk and memory forensics, and phishing triage.

courses.name: Detection engineering and threat hunting
courses.blurb: Write detections instead of just reading alerts: ATT&CK mapping, Sigma and YARA rules, and hypothesis-driven hunts.

modules.note: Finish by writing one hunt in the template from the chapter and a Sigma rule that would have caught what you found.

courses.name: Governance, risk and compliance
courses.blurb: Frameworks (NIST CSF, 800-53, ISO 27001), risk math and the register, policy writing, audits, privacy law and professional ethics. Extends Security+ domain 5, with a risk worksheet that saves in your browser.

courses.name: Reverse engineering and malware
courses.blurb: Assembly, the PE format, disassemblers, safe malware handling, and extra labs in dynamic analysis, unpacking and reading check functions.

courses.name: Cryptography and mobile security
courses.blurb: How the primitives work and fail: cipher modes, RSA and ECC, TLS and PKI, classic attacks, and how mobile apps store secrets and talk to servers.

modules.note: Cryptopals is coding practice and goes beyond the quiz. Sets 1 and 2 cover the ECB, CBC and nonce attacks from this module.

courses.name: Secure development
courses.blurb: Threat modeling, SAST and DAST, dependency and secret scanning, and the web flaws developers must prevent.

courses.name: Binary exploitation
courses.blurb: How memory bugs become control of a program and how mitigations stop them: stack overflows, format strings, canaries, ASLR and ROP. Toy programs only, in a lab.

courses.name: Web application security
courses.blurb: Defensive-minded web testing: the OWASP Top 10, Burp workflow, injection, XSS, authentication, access control, CSRF, SSRF and APIs. Every lab uses a made-up app.

courses.name: Penetration testing
courses.blurb: How a professional test runs: scope and rules of engagement, enumeration, Linux and Windows privilege escalation, Active Directory attack paths and detections, pivoting and reporting. Fictional networks only.
